abstract_text:
Project Summary / Abstract
Epilepsy, defined by recurrent, unprovoked seizures, affects 1 in 26 people. Generalized epilepsy, which is
20% of all epilepsy, involves seizures that begin in both sides of the brain at once. These seizures have spike
wave discharge correlates on electroencephalogram (EEG), in which the spikes reflect neuronal
hypersynchrony (excessively correlated firing of neurons, both within and between the bilateral cortices).
Severe forms of generalized epilepsy involve seizures that become more frequent over time (epilepsy
progression), which is thought to result from hypersynchrony. Standard therapies targeting neuronal excitability
and synaptic transmission are only partially effective, leading to gaps in care and early mortality. We
discovered that seizure-induced myelin plasticity can promote generalized epilepsy progression
(Knowles et al, Nature Neuroscience, 2022). Myelin plasticity occurs when repetitive patterns of neuronal
activity induce changes in myelin sheath structure. In the healthy brain, myelin plasticity is required for learning
and adaptation. However, we found that in a mouse model of progressive generalized epilepsy (Scn8a+/-),
repetitive seizures also induce myelination, primarily in the corpus callosum. Suppression of myelin plasticity
by selective deletion of TrkB receptors from oligodendrocyte precursor cells (OPCs) in Scn8a+/- TrkB OPC
cKO mice prevented epilepsy progression. Seizure-induced myelination through oligodendroglial BDNF-to-
TrkB signaling (which induces OPC proliferation and differentiation to oligodendrocytes) may thus be a
fundamental mechanism in multiple forms of epilepsy. We hypothesize that seizure-induced callosal
myelination promotes cortical hypersynchrony and generalized epilepsy progression, through BDNF-
induced transcription in OPCs. In Aim 1, we will test the role of seizure-induced callosal myelin plasticity in
cortical hypersynchrony, using innovative brain slice physiology and in vivo calcium imaging approaches. In
Aim 2, we will use single nucleus RNA sequencing and spatial transcriptomics to determine transcriptional
regulation of seizure-induced oligodendrogenesis and epilepsy progression. In Aim 3, we will determine
whether seizure-induced myelin plasticity promotes epilepsy progression in a second genetic model of severe
generalized epilepsy, Gabrb3+/D120N, using MRI myelin mapping and conditional, inducible deletion of TrkB
receptors from OPCs. This work will establish myelin plasticity as a novel pathogenic mechanism in severe
generalized epilepsy, opening new avenues for therapeutic intervention.
project_title: Myelin Plasticity: A Novel Mechanism of Generalized Epilepsy
phr_text:
Project Narrative
Severe generalized epilepsy involves repeated, unprovoked seizures that become more frequent over time
(epilepsy progression), which can lead to early death. We previously discovered a new mechanism of epilepsy
progression in the Scn8a+/- mouse model of generalized epilepsy: seizures induce new myelination within the
seizure network, and seizure-induced myelination promotes further seizures. To determine how this process
occurs, how it may be stopped and the applicability of seizure-induced myelination in multiple genetic forms of
generalized epilepsy, we propose experiments to: (1) determine how seizure-induced myelination influences
neural circuit dynamics, (2) identify underlying transcriptional mechanisms in oligodendroglial cells, and (3)
determine whether seizure-induced myelination occurs in a second genetic model of generalized epilepsy,
Gabrb3+/D120N.
